chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 111 to 120, Ammuvanar's neythal decade spoken by the heroine to her friend (தோழிக்கு உரைத்த பத்து): each poem opens அம்ம வாழி தோழி and sets one moment of the shore love, from the baited kayal and the fear of parting, through gossip, the mother's guard and the closing lilies of evening, to anger that relents and shoulders that bloom again when he comes.

111.reading: The woman tells her friend that she could not live parted from her bond with the lord of the ford where the fisherman fixes bait on a line at the edge of the winding backwater and kills the roe-heavy kayal, since she is not one who can carry out hard penance.
111.nuance: Separation is measured against தவம்: to live apart from him would take an ascetic's power to bear pain, and she says she has none (ஆற்றாதேமே). பாணன் here is the fisher of the shore, not the bard; the fish killed is one that carries roe, so the catch destroys more than itself.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater, the angler and the ford lord fix the shore

comparisons.tenor: the lover's bond that drew her in and will undo her if it breaks

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the angling of her own shore, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

112.reading: The woman tells her friend that they will see the lord of the dark backwater, where green-leaved serunthi spreads, come in person, and tells her modest heart that they have surely forgotten (their shame).
112.nuance: The heart is addressed as நாணுடை, the one that owns modesty, at the moment she tells it the modesty is gone: she will stand and watch him come. What was forgotten is not named, and the last line was repaired in our text, so the sense is not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: the serunthi of the backwater and the shore lord fix the land

113.reading: The woman tells her friend that yesterday the townsfolk spoke of her as the woman of the lord of the ford where high waves break the white sand; hearing it, her mother called her, and she answered softly that it was only a fever.
113.nuance: வெம்மை, heat or fever, is her cover: she gives the mother the love's bodily sign and keeps back its cause. The mother says only அன்னாய், and the girl's பைபய, slowly, is the whole art of the concealment.

thinai_evidence.note: the high waves on white sand and the ford lord fix the shore

114.reading: The woman asks her friend whether, even if the man of the shore does not consent, they should go to his country, where the sea stork cries on the frond-thick palmyra.
114.nuance: Kalavu sends the man to the woman's shore; here the woman proposes crossing to his, unasked (நேரேம் ஆயினும்). All she pictures of his land is a bird crying on a palm, so it is already a place of her own longing; the stork only cries, so it is scene, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea stork and the palmyra are things of the shore

115.reading: The woman tells her friend that the lord of the cool ford, who played with them on the shore of fine sand, has come in hiding and stands at the hard guard their mother keeps.
115.nuance: The day's open play on the sand (நம்மோடு ஆடிய) is set against the secret approach (மறைஇ); the mother's strict guard (அருங்கடி), meant to keep him out, has become the very place where he stands.

thinai_evidence.note: the sandy bank and the ford lord fix the shore

116.reading: The woman tells her friend that while they weep, the evening in which the blue lilies of the dark backwater close has surely come, driving before it a morning that was like it.
116.nuance: The closing lily marks the hour as the woman's own eyes are wet (நாம் அழ). Line 4 can be read as evening having pushed the morning before it, so that even the morning was evening for her; the repeated காலை is hard to fix, and the comparison rests on that reading.

thinai_evidence.note: backwater and evening, the neythal land and hour

comparisons.tenor: the morning that came before the evening and was no kinder

117.reading: The woman tells her friend that it is cruel that beauty should come to this in those who cannot forget the lord of the gem-clear shore, where the punnai's ornament flowers draw patterns at every ford.
117.nuance: The punnai adorns every ford of his shore while her own beauty is spent. She calls the condition cruel (கொடிதே), not the man, and speaks of herself in the general plural, those who do not forget.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai of the fords and the shore lord fix the land

118.reading: The woman tells her friend that today, on seeing the man without justice, she went meaning to rage at him and hold him back, but thinking it over she relented and came away.
118.nuance: அறனிலாளன், the man without aram, is her charge, and line 3 lists what she meant to do; line 4 undoes it. Whether she pitied him or herself (இரங்கி) is left open. The poem stands in a neythal decade, but its situation is the quarrel of the fields, so my thinai differs from the colophon.

thinai_evidence.note: anger at the man that gives way to relenting is oodal, the situation of the fields; the poem names no land

119.reading: The woman tells her friend that the lord of the soft shore land who does not come is surely without love, and greatly so, having in his lack of understanding held to things foreign to them.
119.nuance: The land is soft (மென்புலம்) and the man is hard; the verdict அன்பிலன் is sharpened with மன்ற and பெரிதே. Whose lack of understanding line 2 names, his or the women's in trusting him, is not fixed by the syntax.

thinai_evidence.note: the soft land and the shore lord fix the neythal

120.reading: The woman tells her friend that her pitiable soft shoulders have grown beautiful again, very much so, because the lord of the soft shore, where the water's ripples spread over the rich dark backwater, has come.
120.nuance: அளிய, pitiable, stays on the shoulders even as they bloom: their beauty is on loan from his presence, and the decade's run of wasting and fear closes on its reversal (வந்த மாறே, because he came).

links.note: Ainkurunuru 111 says she cannot live parted because she cannot do hard penance (அருந்தவம் முயறல் ஆற்றாதேமே); Kuruntokai 344 says those who see their lovers return must have done penance (நோற்றோர் மன்ற).
links.teaches: In one poem penance is the endurance a woman would need to survive separation, in the other the merit that earns the lover's return, so Sangam akam uses tapas both as a power to bear absence and as the price of its ending.

links.note: Kural 261 defines தவம் as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life; Ainkurunuru 111's woman says she is no performer of hard penance and so could not live apart from him.
links.teaches: The heroine's disclaimer assumes exactly the Kural's definition of penance as the bearing of suffering, so the pair shows that the endurance of separation was already counted as an ascetic feat, and that the lover's refusal of it is a refusal of tapas.

links.note: Both are the woman's own words: Kural 1257 says she knows nothing called modesty when the beloved does what love wants; Ainkurunuru 112 tells her modest heart they have forgotten, as they wait to see him come.
links.teaches: The Kural's general claim that shame vanishes before love is shown in the poem as a single moment, the heroine speaking to the heart that owns modesty just as she gives it up to watch him arrive.

links.note: Both pair the town's gossip with the mother's word: Kural 1147 says gossip is manure and mother's words water to this sickness; in Ainkurunuru 113 the town names her the lord's woman, mother calls her, and she says it is only a fever (வெம்மை).
links.teaches: The Kural calls the love a sickness that gossip and the mother feed, and the poem shows the girl turning that very likeness into her alibi, naming the fever and hiding its cause, so the couplet's metaphor began as the lover's cover story.

links.note: Kural 1225 asks what good she did to morning and what harm to evening; Ainkurunuru 116 has evening come while they weep, having driven before it a morning like itself.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps a kind morning against a hostile evening, while the older poem, on one reading, lets the evening swallow the morning too, so the couplet's neat split of the day is a later tidying of a grief that had no safe hour.

links.note: Kural 1235 has the wasted shoulders declare the cruelty of the cruel man (கொடியார் கொடுமை); in Ainkurunuru 117 the woman says it is cruel (கொடிதே) that beauty comes to this in those who do not forget him.
links.teaches: The friend in the Kural lays the cruelty on the man, while the heroine in the poem lays it on the condition of loving him, so the same lost beauty is a charge against him from outside and a lament without an accused from within.

links.note: Kural 1284: she went to sulk, but her heart forgot it and went to unite; Ainkurunuru 118: she went meaning to rage at the unjust man and hold him back, but thought again, relented and came away.
links.teaches: Both women set out angry and lose the anger on the way, but the Kural's anger turns into union while the Sangam heroine's turns into retreat, so a failed quarrel need not end in an embrace: it can end in pity and silence.

links.note: Kural 1265 wishes to see the கொண்கன் with full eyes so that the pallor of her soft shoulders (மென்தோள்) may leave; Ainkurunuru 120 reports that her soft shoulders (மெல் தோளே) have become beautiful because the lord has come.
links.teaches: The Kural states as a hope that the sight of the shore lord will cure the shoulders, and the Ainkurunuru records the cure as done, so the couplet's optative has an older poem in which the wish was already fulfilled.

source_issues: 111-120: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade, so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the decade title and the poem.
112: line 4 (மறந்தோம் மன்ற நாணுடை நெஞ்சே) is a repaired line in our text; what is forgotten is not stated, and the sense is marked uncertain.
116: line 4 (காலை யன்ன காலைமுந் துறுத்தே) repeats காலை and is hard to construe; the reading is marked uncertain.
118: line 3 is the tamilvu.org reading, agreeing with sangamtamil.com; no doubt remains about the words.
118: the colophon thinai is நெய்தல் but the poem names no land and its situation is oodal; my thinai is marutham.
